what_it_does: In a giant cloud data center, figuring out which physical server should host each new virtual machine (VM — a software-emulated computer rented by a customer) is an optimization problem with no perfect solution, made harder because no one knows in advance how long each VM will run. LAVA is Google's production system that predicts not just how long a VM will run at birth, but keeps revising that prediction throughout the VM's life — allowing the scheduler to correct early mistakes — and this continuous re-prediction meaningfully increases the fraction of servers that become completely empty (useful for large VMs and energy savings).
method_in_detail:
The idea. Fragmentation — servers that have some free space but not enough for any new VM — wastes capacity. Prior work predicted each VM's lifespan once at creation and used that prediction to group VMs with similar lifetimes together. But a single wrong prediction on even one VM can strand a whole server for weeks. The key insight here is that as a VM keeps running, you learn more about it: a VM that was supposed to last an hour but is still alive after two days is almost certainly going to run for much longer, and a second prediction made with that knowledge is far more accurate.

The model. A gradient-boosted decision tree (a fast, accurate tree-based machine learning model) takes as input the VM's properties (machine type, zone, whether it has a local SSD, project metadata) plus its current uptime. The model outputs the expected remaining lifetime given observed uptime — effectively a survival curve collapsed to a single number. Training data is augmented by turning each historical VM into multiple training examples at different uptime fractions, teaching the model to reason conditionally. The model is compiled directly into the scheduler binary, cutting inference latency to under 10 microseconds — 780x faster than a separate model-serving approach — which is what makes frequent re-prediction practical.

Three algorithms built on this. NILAS is 'non-invasive': when several servers score equally well on other metrics, it breaks the tie by preferring the server whose current VMs are predicted to exit latest (matching the new VM's expected exit time), using re-predicted rather than stale initial predictions. LAVA is more aggressive: servers are classified into lifetime buckets (under 1 hour, 1–10 hours, 10–100 hours, 100–1000 hours). A server fills up with VMs of its class, then transitions to 'recycling' mode where only shorter-lived VMs are accepted — so that the server will gradually empty as shorter VMs exit even if a long-lived residual VM remains. When a misprediction is detected (a VM outlives its server's expected deadline), the server's class is bumped up; when VMs vacate faster than expected, the class steps down. LARS applies lifetime predictions to the order in which VMs are migrated during maintenance, moving the longest-predicted VMs first so shorter ones can naturally exit while longer ones are still being moved.

The key design choice. Treating predictions as distributions (survival curves) rather than point estimates, and re-running the model throughout each VM's life, opens up a qualitatively different class of scheduling decisions that one-shot prediction cannot make.

The result. Fleet-wide production deployment at Google: empty hosts increased by 2.3–9.2 percentage points (1 pp is equivalent to 1% of cluster capacity), CPU stranding reduced by ~3%, memory stranding by ~2%, live migrations reduced by ~4.5%.
